title: UNIQUE
description: Declare single and composite uniqueness at the intended grain, account for NULL and collation rules, and distinguish deduplicating proposed input from enforcing accepted state.
notes:
## Uniqueness protects a stated value combination

A UNIQUE constraint requires an accepted set of column values to obey the engine's uniqueness rules. A campus service might require each supplied contact code to identify at most one account, while still using account_id as the primary key. The unique property expresses a business rule about another value role, rather than turning every descriptive label into an identifier.

Start by stating what must not repeat. If an enrollment permits one accepted row per student and course pair, the combination is unique. The same student may still appear with different courses, and the same course may appear with different students. Confusing pair uniqueness with separate uniqueness on each component accidentally changes a many-to-many participation model into a much stricter one.

## Column and table forms express different shapes

A single-column rule can appear with that column's definition or in a suitable table-level declaration. A composite rule lists the participating columns together in the appropriate table-level form. Two separate UNIQUE declarations are not equivalent to one UNIQUE(student_id, course_id) declaration. The separate declarations each reject repeated component values independently.

For example, pairs (1,10), (1,20) and (2,10) satisfy pair uniqueness even though student 1 and course 10 recur. A second (1,10) violates that pair rule. This concrete trace is more useful than memorizing syntax without a population model. Write the accepted grain in ordinary language before deciding which columns belong in the constraint.

```sql
CREATE TABLE accepted_enrollments (
  student_id INT NOT NULL,
  course_id INT NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT uq_student_course UNIQUE (student_id, course_id)
);
```

## Presence and uniqueness are separate decisions

A nullable unique contact field may allow several missing values under the illustrated MySQL rules. That does not mean those rows share one known contact value. It means an absent marker is handled differently from repeated ordinary values by the uniqueness mechanism. If every row must provide the property, add the required presence rule explicitly.

PostgreSQL also supports configurable NULL-distinctness behaviour in applicable unique definitions, including NULLS NOT DISTINCT. Therefore an explanation saying NULL is never treated alike for uniqueness everywhere is inaccurate. State the product, version and chosen rule. The exercises use ordinary MySQL nullable-unique behaviour for one task and required pair components for the other.

## String comparison rules define what counts as duplicate

Unique text values are compared under the relevant type and collation rules. Two spellings differing only in case may conflict under one collation and remain distinct under another. Domain expectations for institutional codes, email-like identifiers or display labels need to match those comparison semantics. A familiar-looking sample does not establish that the chosen rules fit every international input.

The fixtures use canonical labels that avoid case and accent ambiguity so their reference outputs are clear. That is an exercise boundary, not a claim that real uniqueness can ignore collation. If a production rule requires case-sensitive identifiers, choose and verify an appropriate definition. Do not try to repair a mismatched comparison policy by adding DISTINCT only to the display query.

## A primary key has an additional identity role

A table can have at most one primary-key constraint, including a composite one, and multiple supported unique constraints. It can also have no declared primary key. Saying every table must declare exactly one is not an accurate description of SQL syntax, even though a well-designed application table often needs a clear primary identity.

PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE with required values overlap in their accepted uniqueness and presence rules, but they are not identical declarations in every operational respect. The primary key identifies the table's designated key and can have engine-specific storage or reference significance. Do not reduce the difference to a universal text substitution that ignores metadata and implementation behaviour.

## Existing duplicates can block a new rule

Adding UNIQUE to a populated column requires its existing values to satisfy the intended rule under the chosen comparison semantics. A proposed change can fail when two accepted rows already conflict. The right response is to identify the domain conflict and its ownership, not silently delete one row or make up another identifier so the DDL appears to succeed.

A diagnostic GROUP BY with a suitable count can expose repeated ordinary values, but NULL and collation interpretation still need to match the intended constraint. Checking an approximate sample is not proof that the full table satisfies the rule. Under a live workload, concurrent writers also need coordination so the state checked during preparation remains compatible with final enforcement.

## Query deduplication does not enforce future writes

SELECT DISTINCT returns a result set without repeated selected tuples. It does not add a constraint to the source or stop another writer from inserting a conflicting accepted row. A report can therefore look clean while the underlying table still violates the intended business rule. Keep result transformation and accepted-state enforcement as different operations.

The second exercise intentionally combines both: proposals can contain repeated student-course pairs, which the task treats as redundant proposals for the same accepted participation. DISTINCT chooses the requested target set, and the target UNIQUE rule protects that accepted set afterward. This is valid because the domain contract explicitly permits collapsing those proposal occurrences; it would be wrong for an event log that must preserve every attempt.

## Handle conflicts according to the requested policy

A duplicate-key error can represent a genuine conflicting submission, a retry of an already accepted request, or a defect in the writer. The application needs to decide which interpretation applies. A constraint establishes the boundary, but it does not decide whether to report a conflict, return an existing result or apply a carefully defined update.

Do not add IGNORE or an upsert merely to hide every duplicate error. Those forms have their own accepted-state semantics and can mask unrelated problems or change data. The exercises use ordinary insertion and explicit negative cases so the boundary remains visible. More advanced conflict handling belongs to its own topic with an equally precise policy and tests.

## Naming helps maintenance but differs by engine

A named uniqueness rule makes the intended invariant easier to discuss and inspect. In MySQL, a unique constraint is backed through an index representation, and dropping the appropriate named unique index is the relevant illustrated form. Other products distinguish constraint-removal syntax differently. Inspect the actual catalog name rather than assume every engine assigns or exposes the same name.

Removing a unique rule changes accepted future writes even when no current rows change. Existing callers may rely on that guarantee for lookup or conflict behaviour. Review the dependency before describing constraint removal as a harmless performance adjustment. An index's maintenance cost is relevant, but it does not justify weakening a required integrity rule merely because writes become cheaper.

## Index cost is a tradeoff within the integrity requirement

Supported unique indexes perform maintenance when relevant rows change. That can contribute to write and storage cost, while also supporting particular lookups. The actual performance effect depends on workload, data distribution and engine behaviour. A tiny fixture cannot establish a production latency benefit or a universal cost ratio for adding a unique rule.

First decide whether the invariant is required. If it is, evaluate supported implementations and workload effects while preserving that contract. If it is not required, avoid adding arbitrary restrictions just because the column seems important. An unnecessary unique constraint can reject legitimate repeated facts, which is a correctness problem before it is a performance consideration.

## Validate pair boundaries and missing values deliberately

The introductory exercise creates a nullable unique contact field and loads rows whose ordinary contacts are distinct. Several NULL contacts remain permitted under the stated rules. A duplicate ordinary contact is rejected separately, making the missing-value distinction observable. A primary id keeps repeated missing contacts attached to distinct account rows.

The composite exercise includes (1,10), (1,20) and (2,10), plus a repeated proposal for (1,10). Its accepted output contains the three distinct pairs. A later duplicate-pair write is rejected, while different combinations remain valid. Empty input creates no invented participation. These cases verify the intended grain more effectively than several copies of one isolated key sample.

## Keep the final claim aligned with the tested definition

A useful illustration shows which repeated components are allowed and which complete tuple conflicts. The notes, MCQs and target DDL should all describe that same rule. This alignment lets the learner explain why a pair constraint differs from two individual constraints and why a unique optional property still needs a separate presence decision.

Recorded MariaDB compatibility fixtures verify the supplied accepted and rejected writes. Exact MySQL/provider collation behaviour, production concurrency and application migration application remain separately unverified. PostgreSQL NULLS NOT DISTINCT is a documented contrast rather than a local native execution claim. The complete package teaches the actual invariant without pretending that uniqueness alone validates every business fact.

questions.question_text: Which SQL clause is required when a uniqueness rule must span two columns together, such as (student_id, course_id)?
options: Two separate column-level UNIQUE clauses, one per column
A table-level UNIQUE clause listing both columns
A CHECK constraint referencing both columns
A FOREIGN KEY referencing both columns
questions.explanation: Column-level UNIQUE applies to a single column only; a composite uniqueness rule requires the table-level UNIQUE (col1, col2) form.

questions.question_text: Under ordinary nullable UNIQUE behaviour in the illustrated MySQL definition, can several rows have NULL?
options: Zero — NULL is forbidden in a UNIQUE column
Exactly one
Yes; repeated missing markers are permitted by this chosen rule
Unlimited only if the column is also indexed manually
questions.explanation: Products and options such as PostgreSQL NULLS NOT DISTINCT can choose different uniqueness treatment.

questions.question_text: What is the correct way to drop a named UNIQUE constraint `uq_users_username` in MySQL?
options: ALTER TABLE users DROP CONSTRAINT uq_users_username;
ALTER TABLE users DROP UNIQUE uq_users_username;
ALTER TABLE users DROP INDEX uq_users_username;
DROP UNIQUE ON users.uq_users_username;
questions.explanation: MySQL implements UNIQUE constraints as unique indexes internally, so they are dropped with DROP INDEX rather than DROP CONSTRAINT.

questions.question_text: What happens when you run ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT uq_username UNIQUE (username); on a table that already has two rows with the same username value?
options: The constraint is added and future duplicates are blocked, but the existing duplicates remain
The statement fails because existing data violates the new constraint
MySQL silently deletes one of the duplicate rows
The constraint is added in a disabled state
questions.explanation: Adding a UNIQUE constraint validates existing data first; duplicates already present cause the ALTER TABLE to be rejected.

questions.question_text: How many primary-key constraints can a table declare?
options: At most one; it may also declare several supported unique rules
Any number of both
Exactly one of each
Any number of PRIMARY KEY, exactly one UNIQUE
questions.explanation: SQL permits a table with no declared primary key.

questions.question_text: How should PRIMARY KEY be distinguished from a required UNIQUE rule?
options: They are unrelated features with no overlap
They overlap in presence and uniqueness but differ in designated key role and possible engine-specific behaviour
UNIQUE is a stricter version of PRIMARY KEY
PRIMARY KEY allows NULLs while UNIQUE does not
questions.explanation: They are not universally identical metadata or storage declarations.

questions.question_text: In a composite constraint UNIQUE (a, b), which of the following is allowed?
options: Duplicate values in column a alone, as long as the (a, b) pair as a whole is not duplicated
Any duplicate row where a matches another row's a
No duplicates in either column individually
Duplicate (a, b) pairs as long as a is not the primary key
questions.explanation: A composite UNIQUE constraint only forbids duplicate combinations of the listed columns; individual columns may repeat freely on their own.

questions.question_text: Why might a database administrator avoid adding a UNIQUE constraint to a column that doesn't strictly need one?
options: UNIQUE constraints prevent the column from ever being updated
UNIQUE automatically creates a supporting index in most engines, adding overhead to write-heavy workloads
UNIQUE constraints cannot coexist with NOT NULL
UNIQUE constraints are deprecated in modern SQL
questions.explanation: Most engines back a UNIQUE constraint with an index to enforce it efficiently, and that index carries maintenance cost on every insert/update, which matters for high-write tables.

questions.question_text: Does UNIQUE(student_id,course_id) forbid a student from taking two different courses?
options: Yes
No
Only if ids are integers
Only on an empty table
questions.explanation: The complete pair, not each component alone, is protected.

questions.question_text: Does SELECT DISTINCT enforce source uniqueness for future writes?
options: Yes
Only when ordered
No
Only with VARCHAR
questions.explanation: A result transformation does not change accepted table state.

questions.question_text: Which pair conflicts with an accepted (1,10)?
options: Another (1,10)
questions.explanation: The protected combination must repeat.

questions.question_text: Why can collation matter for a unique code?
options: It grants all users access
It automatically chooses business identity
It removes every constraint
It determines relevant string comparison behaviour
questions.explanation: Case and accent treatment can affect duplicate interpretation.

questions.question_text: Can a SQL table omit a declared primary key?
options: Yes
No
Only if empty
Only with no text
questions.explanation: At most one is different from exactly one required declaration.

questions.question_text: What should happen before resolving existing duplicate accepted identities?
options: Silent arbitrary deletion
A domain decision about the conflicting facts
Random key invention
Only a report alias
questions.explanation: DDL success is not a valid reason to discard legitimate data.

questions.question_text: Why does the proposal-copy exercise use DISTINCT?
options: All event logs should lose duplicates
UNIQUE always deletes duplicates first
Its contract treats repeated pair proposals as the same accepted participation
It changes every id
questions.explanation: The target set grain is explicitly requested.

questions.question_text: Does a unique nullable contact necessarily require a contact on every row?
options: Yes
Only if the contact is long
Only with an index name
No
questions.explanation: Presence is a separate requirement.

questions.question_text: What does dropping a required unique index change?
options: The future integrity boundary as well as index maintenance
Only note formatting
No behaviour
Only output order
questions.explanation: Callers may rely on duplicate rejection.

questions.question_text: Does a duplicate error prescribe one universal application response?
options: Yes, always ignore it
No
Yes, always delete the old row
Yes, always overwrite
questions.explanation: Retries, conflicting requests and defects need a policy.

questions.question_text: What does one successful sample fail to establish?
options: Its recorded reference output
The supplied accepted pair set
Production concurrency and every collation boundary
A tested duplicate rejection
questions.explanation: Evidence has a defined scope.

questions.question_text: Why not add uniqueness to every important label?
options: Every label is globally unique
It always improves correctness
It has no acceptance effect
Legitimate repeated descriptions may be allowed
questions.explanation: A constraint must represent an actual invariant.

coding_problems.title: Enforce unique supplied contacts while permitting missing ones
coding_problems.task: Create TEMPORARY accounts(account_id INT PRIMARY KEY,contact VARCHAR(80) NULL,CONSTRAINT uq_contact UNIQUE(contact)). Copy account_input and return account_id,contact. The ordinary MySQL-style nullable unique rule permits multiple NULL contacts; ordinary supplied contacts in every positive fixture are distinct.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE account_input (account_id INT PRIMARY KEY,contact VARCHAR(80) NULL);
edge_cases: Several NULL contacts remain separate account rows.
A repeated ordinary contact is rejected.
hints: Use a separate primary identity and nullable unique contact role.
Do not deduplicate account rows merely because contact is absent.
coding_problems.solution_sql: CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE accounts (account_id INT PRIMARY KEY,contact VARCHAR(80) NULL,CONSTRAINT uq_contact UNIQUE(contact)); INSERT INTO accounts SELECT account_id,contact FROM account_input; SELECT account_id,contact FROM accounts ORDER BY account_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The unique rule applies to supplied contact values under the stated engine rules while primary identity preserves distinct accounts.

coding_problems.title: Accept a pair set and protect future composite uniqueness
coding_problems.task: Create TEMPORARY accepted_enrollments with student_id INT NOT NULL,course_id INT NOT NULL and UNIQUE(student_id,course_id). Treat proposals as a set of requested participations: copy each distinct pair exactly once. Return the accepted pairs. A repeated student with another course and a repeated course with another student are permitted.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE proposals (student_id INT NOT NULL,course_id INT NOT NULL);
constraints: Proposal occurrences intentionally collapse to the requested pair set.
The accepted target enforces complete pair uniqueness.
edge_cases: Component repetition is allowed when the full pair differs.
A duplicate accepted pair is rejected.
hints: List both columns together in one unique rule.
Use DISTINCT to implement this proposal-to-set policy.
coding_problems.solution_sql: CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE accepted_enrollments (student_id INT NOT NULL,course_id INT NOT NULL,CONSTRAINT uq_student_course UNIQUE(student_id,course_id)); INSERT INTO accepted_enrollments SELECT DISTINCT student_id,course_id FROM proposals; SELECT student_id,course_id FROM accepted_enrollments ORDER BY student_id,course_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The copy defines an accepted pair set and the constraint preserves that invariant for future writes.

original_questions.question_text: In standard PostgreSQL behavior, how many rows can have NULL in a UNIQUE column?
options: Zero — NULL is forbidden in a UNIQUE column
Exactly one
Multiple rows, since NULL is never considered equal to another NULL
Unlimited only if the column is also indexed manually
original_questions.explanation: PostgreSQL, like MySQL and Oracle, treats each NULL as an unknown value, so multiple NULLs don't violate uniqueness; SQL Server differs and allows only one.

original_questions.question_text: What is the correct way to drop a named UNIQUE constraint `uq_users_username` in MySQL?
options: ALTER TABLE users DROP CONSTRAINT uq_users_username;
ALTER TABLE users DROP UNIQUE uq_users_username;
ALTER TABLE users DROP INDEX uq_users_username;
DROP UNIQUE ON users.uq_users_username;
original_questions.explanation: MySQL implements UNIQUE constraints as unique indexes internally, so they are dropped with DROP INDEX rather than DROP CONSTRAINT.

original_questions.question_text: What happens when you run ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT uq_username UNIQUE (username); on a table that already has two rows with the same username value?
options: The constraint is added and future duplicates are blocked, but the existing duplicates remain
The statement fails because existing data violates the new constraint
MySQL silently deletes one of the duplicate rows
The constraint is added in a disabled state

original_questions.question_text: How many PRIMARY KEY constraints and how many UNIQUE constraints can a single table have?
options: Exactly one PRIMARY KEY, and any number of UNIQUE constraints
Any number of both
Exactly one of each
Any number of PRIMARY KEY, exactly one UNIQUE
original_questions.explanation: A table has at most one PRIMARY KEY but can define multiple UNIQUE constraints on different columns or column combinations.

original_questions.question_text: Which best describes the relationship between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE at the syntax/semantics level?
options: They are unrelated features with no overlap
PRIMARY KEY is equivalent to UNIQUE plus NOT NULL bundled together
UNIQUE is a stricter version of PRIMARY KEY
PRIMARY KEY allows NULLs while UNIQUE does not
original_questions.explanation: A PRIMARY KEY combines the uniqueness guarantee of UNIQUE with an implicit NOT NULL, which is why PRIMARY KEY columns can never contain NULL.

Any duplicate row where a matches another row's a
No duplicates in either column individually
Duplicate (a, b) pairs as long as a is not the primary key
original_questions.explanation: A composite UNIQUE constraint only forbids duplicate combinations of the listed columns; individual columns may repeat freely on their own.
